value: The variant graph data model used to represent text collations, and whether its constraints can be expressed formally.
Can a graph-based scholarly data model be validated with the same rigour as a TEI XML or relational schema?
Shows where OWL fails as a validation language for graph data, and what a constraint language has to do instead.

quote: Recently, however, there have been two intriguing developments in the Semantic Web world that are especially relevant to digital humanities projects, not least Stemmarest.

This language solves exactly the problem that ontologies do not; specifically, in conjunction with a database that supports transactions and their rollbacks such as Neo4J, a set of SHACL constraints can ensure the consistency of data added to the graph, so that (to take the example above) a witness from one text tradition cannot be included in a stemma belonging to an entirely different tradition.
In this sense, the critics of graph-based models do have a point; how do we validate our graphs?

quote: Thus, while the Stemmarest ontology can describe the data reasonably well, it is not an adequate tool for setting constraints; these must still be described in code.

value: The hard constraints are cross-object: an entity appearing in one structure must be consistent with its membership elsewhere
quote: For example, if a witness W appears in a stemma belonging to tradition A, the model software should ensure that W also belongs to tradition A as a witness and not, for example, an unrelated tradition B; moreover, W should not appear in any stemmata of tradition B.

value: Some constraints are global properties of the whole graph and cannot be checked object by object at all
quote: Even more intractable problems arise with more complex specifications: for example, the need to ensure that the variant graph is self-consistent, so that a user cannot create a situation in the model where a portion of the edited text loops back onto itself or is omitted altogether.

value: The original failure was not a modelling mistake but a mismatch of purpose - OWL was built for open-world inference and editors want description and consistency
quote: We would argue here that most editors are less interested in the sort of open-world inference for which OWL was intended (though Vogeler makes a case for why it might be interesting), as opposed to the formalisation, description, and consistency of their data.

RDF*, an extension to RDF that allows an entire triple to be the subject or object in further triple statements
